--- title: "Black boxes and interpretable models" description: "Seven models on the same folds. The most interpretable flexible model is also the most accurate, which means the usual trade-off is not the one being made." order: 3 categories: [interpretation, metrics] --- ## Why this matters The standard framing is a trade-off: interpretable models are transparent but weak, black boxes are accurate but opaque, and you choose according to whether you need to explain or to predict. Reviewers ask for it in those terms. Talks are built around it. On tabular ecological data the trade-off is usually smaller than advertised, and sometimes it runs the other way. This page measures it on the coastal survey, with all seven models scored on identical folds. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ## Scoring them fairly Two conventions from §7 do the work here. Every model sees **the same resamples**, so the comparison is paired rather than seven independent estimates. And we **pool the out-of-fold predictions** before computing a metric, so every model is scored on exactly the same 720 rows. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean() modelling <- survey |> select(abundance, depth_m, temperature_c, chlorophyll_mg_m3, salinity_psu, substrate, season, longitude, latitude) |> drop_na() set.seed(9) folds <- vfold_cv(modelling, v = 10) out_of_fold <- function(fit_one, predict_one) { map_dfr(folds$splits, \(split) { fitted <- fit_one(analysis(split)) held <- assessment(split) tibble(truth = held$abundance, prediction = predict_one(fitted, held)) }) } ``` ::: The seven span the range from "no model at all" to "no interpretation at all". ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} tree_spec <- function(spec) { list(fit = \(data) fit(workflow() |> add_recipe(recipe(abundance ~ ., data = data) |> step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors())) |> add_model(spec), data), predict = \(m, x) predict(m, x)$.pred) } forest <- tree_spec(rand_forest(trees = 800) |> set_engine("ranger", seed = 1) |> set_mode("regression")) boosted <- tree_spec(boost_tree(trees = 400, learn_rate = 0.05, tree_depth = 4) |> set_engine("xgboost") |> set_mode("regression")) gam_formula <- abundance ~ s(depth_m, k = 8) + s(temperature_c, k = 8) + s(chlorophyll_mg_m3, k = 8) + s(longitude, latitude, k = 30) + substrate + season + salinity_psu glm_formula <- abundance ~ poly(depth_m, 2, raw = TRUE) + poly(temperature_c, 2, raw = TRUE) + log1p(chlorophyll_mg_m3) + substrate + season + salinity_psu results <- list( `mean only` = out_of_fold(\(a) mean(a$abundance), \(m, x) rep(m, nrow(x))), `linear regression` = out_of_fold(\(a) lm(abundance ~ ., data = a), \(m, x) predict(m, x)), `negative binomial GLM, linear terms` = out_of_fold(\(a) MASS::glm.nb(abundance ~ ., data = a), \(m, x) predict(m, x, type = "response")), `negative binomial GLM, correct form` = out_of_fold(\(a) MASS::glm.nb(glm_formula, data = a), \(m, x) predict(m, x, type = "response")), `GAM with smooth terms` = out_of_fold(\(a) gam(gam_formula, family = nb(), data = a), \(m, x) as.numeric(predict(m, x, type = "response"))), `random forest` = out_of_fold(forest$fit, forest$predict), `boosted trees` = out_of_fold(boosted$fit, boosted$predict) ) imap_dfr(results, \(scored, name) { tibble(model = name, RMSE = rmse_vec(scored$truth, scored$prediction), MAE = mae_vec(scored$truth, scored$prediction), `survey total, % error` = 100 * (sum(scored$prediction) - sum(scored$truth)) / sum(scored$truth)) }) |> arrange(RMSE) |> mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 2))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|model | RMSE| MAE| survey total, % error| |:-----------------------------------|----:|----:|---------------------:| |GAM with smooth terms | 4.08| 2.79| -1.50| |negative binomial GLM, correct form | 4.25| 2.90| -0.33| |random forest | 4.28| 2.96| 3.13| |negative binomial GLM, linear terms | 4.38| 3.06| -0.53| |linear regression | 4.41| 3.13| -0.58| |boosted trees | 4.74| 3.15| 2.34| |mean only | 4.82| 3.41| 0.00|
::: ::: ## The trade-off did not happen The **GAM wins**, on RMSE and on MAE, and it is the second most interpretable model in the list. The random forest is third, behind a negative-binomial GLM given the right functional form. The boosted trees come sixth of seven on RMSE, above only predicting the mean. For scale: an oracle that knows every station's true expected count scores 3.93 on these rows, and the mean-only baseline scores 4.82. The GAM at 4.08 closes about **83%** of that gap; the random forest closes about 60%. This is not a surprising result if you know what is in the generator. The truth is two smooth humped responses, a saturating effect, four substrate levels and a smooth spatial field. That is precisely the class of model a GAM is: smooth additive terms and a spatial smoother. The GAM won because it was right about the shape of the world. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Why the boosted trees did so badly `boost_tree()` with 400 rounds and no tuning overfits a noisy count response, and unlike a random forest it has no averaging to protect it. §5's [hyperparameter selection](../05-generalisation/hyperparameter-selection.qmd) would fix most of that. It is included untuned deliberately: the comparison people actually run is default against default, and this is what that looks like. ::: ## What interpretability actually buys It is not just the ranking. Here is the GAM's own summary, which comes free with the fit. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} full_gam <- gam(gam_formula, family = nb(), data = modelling) summary(full_gam)$s.table |> as_tibble(rownames = "smooth term") |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) signif(x, 3))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|smooth term | edf| Ref.df| Chi.sq| p-value| |:---------------------|-----:|------:|------:|-------:| |s(depth_m) | 3.29| 4.10| 8.84| 0.06090| |s(temperature_c) | 4.64| 5.55| 116.00| 0.00000| |s(chlorophyll_mg_m3) | 1.00| 1.00| 6.44| 0.01130| |s(longitude,latitude) | 10.70| 14.80| 35.50| 0.00193|
::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} summary(full_gam)$p.table |> as_tibble(rownames = "term") |> filter(str_starts(term, "substrate") | term == "salinity_psu") |> mutate(`true value (vs gravel)` = c(0.20, -0.80, -0.20, 0), across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 3))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|term | Estimate| Std. Error| z value| Pr(>|z|)| true value (vs gravel)| |:-------------|--------:|----------:|-------:|------------------:|----------------------:| |substratemud | 0.170| 0.109| 1.564| 0.118| 0.2| |substraterock | -0.479| 0.177| -2.712| 0.007| -0.8| |substratesand | -0.237| 0.109| -2.177| 0.029| -0.2| |salinity_psu | 0.064| 0.121| 0.527| 0.598| 0.0|
::: ::: Every line of that is a scientific statement with an uncertainty attached. - **Temperature** has 4.6 effective degrees of freedom and a $\chi^2$ of 116: strongly nonlinear and the dominant term. - **Chlorophyll** has 1.0 effective degrees of freedom — the GAM has decided the effect is linear on the link scale — and $p = 0.011$. Recall that [permutation importance put chlorophyll inside the noise band](feature-importance.qmd). A model that *estimates an effect* and a measure that *quantifies reliance* are answering different questions, and here they disagree completely. - **The spatial smoother** takes 10.7 degrees of freedom and is significant, which is the correct detection of a field no covariate explains. - **Substrate** comes back as mud > gravel > sand > rock, with estimates of 0.17, 0, −0.24 and −0.48 against true values of 0.20, 0, −0.20 and −0.80. The ordering is exactly right. Recall that [impurity importance ranked substrate below three columns of random numbers](feature-importance.qmd). - **Salinity** is 0.064 ± 0.122, $p = 0.60$ — correctly identified as nothing, which is the truth. You can also read the shapes straight off, with intervals. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} smooth_frame <- function(variable, true_function) { grid <- seq(min(modelling[[variable]]), max(modelling[[variable]]), length.out = 200) newdata <- modelling[rep(1, 200), ] newdata[[variable]] <- grid terms <- predict(full_gam, newdata, type = "terms", se.fit = TRUE) column <- paste0("s(", variable, ")") truth <- true_function(grid) tibble(x = grid, fit = terms$fit[, column], se = terms$se.fit[, column], truth = truth - mean(true_function(modelling[[variable]]))) } smooth_panel <- function(frame, label, marker) { ggplot(frame, aes(x, fit)) + geom_vline(xintercept = marker, linetype = "dashed", colour = "#e6eaed") + geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = fit - 1.96 * se, ymax = fit + 1.96 * se), fill = ml_palette[["blue"]], alpha = 0.18) + geom_line(colour = ml_palette[["blue"]], linewidth = 0.9) + geom_line(aes(y = truth), linetype = "dashed", colour = ml_palette[["vermilion"]], linewidth = 0.8) + labs(x = label, y = "effect on log expected count") } (smooth_panel(smooth_frame("temperature_c", \(t) -0.60 * ((t - 9) / 3)^2), "temperature (°C)", 9) | smooth_panel(smooth_frame("depth_m", \(d) -0.55 * ((d - 80) / 60)^2), "depth (m)", 80)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The GAM's fitted smooth terms with 95% intervals, against the true curves from the generator (both centred, so only the shape is compared). Temperature is recovered with the right amplitude and its peak one degree early. The depth smooth is flatter than the truth and peaks at 52 m rather than 80 — but its interval contains the true curve at 197 of 200 grid points, and is wide enough to contain a flat line everywhere shallower than 155 m.](black-box-or-not_files/figure-html/fig-smooths-1.png){#fig-smooths fig-alt='Two panels on the link scale, each with a solid fitted line, a shaded 95% interval and a dashed true curve. In the temperature panel the fitted smooth rises from about minus 2.5 at two degrees to a maximum just above zero near eight, then falls to about minus 2 at sixteen; the dashed true curve runs very close to it throughout, peaking one degree later. The interval is narrow in the middle and widens sharply at both ends. In the depth panel the fitted smooth is a broad flat-topped hump, rising gently from about minus 0.1 at five metres to a shallow maximum near fifty, staying level to about a hundred and ten, then declining to about minus 1.2 at the deepest stations; the dashed true curve is a more pronounced hump peaking at eighty metres and dropping lower at both ends, and it lies inside the shaded interval almost everywhere.' width=1900} ::: ::: ## What the depth panel is actually saying Look at depth before concluding either that the interpretable model solved the problem or that it failed. Its smooth peaks at 52 m rather than 80, it is flatter than the truth, and $p = 0.061$. Read that as a failure and you would be missing the point. The interval covers the true curve at **197 of 200 grid points**. What the GAM has produced is not a wrong answer; it is a *wide* one. And it is specific about where the width is: zero is excluded only beyond 155 m, so the model is confident there is a decline at the deep end and openly unsure about everything shallower. Compare that with [the previous page](partial-effects.qmd), where the same confounding made the forest's partial dependence a confident-looking monotone decline with no uncertainty attached at all, and the quadratic GLM's an even steeper one. Same data, same non-identifiability, three presentations: one silently wrong, one silently wrong, one visibly uncertain. **That is what interpretability buys, and it is not correctness.** It is the ability of a model to tell you that the data cannot answer your question. A partial-dependence plot has no mechanism for saying so. ## So when is a black box worth it? The measured case for one, from this course: - **When the structure is not additive and not smooth.** §9's [water-mass band](../09-neural-networks/when-to-use-one.qmd) is a diagonal interaction where 17 network weights beat a 500-tree forest and logistic regression never exceeded AUC 0.72. A GAM with additive smooths would fail there too. - **When you have no idea what the form is.** The GAM won here because smooth-additive is the right family. Choose it wrongly — the linear-terms GLM at 4.38 — and you give up the accuracy you thought interpretability was costing you. A forest is insurance against not knowing. - **When the inputs are raw.** Pixels, spectra and waveforms have no interpretable coefficients to give up, so there is no trade-off to make. - **When prediction is genuinely the product.** A survey-design tool or an operational forecast is judged on its predictions. §1's [prediction versus explanation](../01-introduction/prediction-and-explanation.qmd) distinction decides which column of the table above you should be reading. And the case against: every method in §10 for getting an effect out of a black box — importance, partial dependence, ALE — is an *approximation* of a quantity a GAM reports directly, with an interval, for free. ## Where this breaks down **One dataset, one generating process.** This survey was built from smooth additive effects, so a smooth additive model was always going to do well. On data with strong interactions the ordering would change, and the way to find out is to run the comparison rather than assume either answer. **The GAM was given a good formula.** `s(longitude, latitude)` is there because §6 showed spatial structure, and `k = 8` is a choice. An interpretable model is only as good as the specification, and the specification is where the domain knowledge goes. **None of these intervals account for model selection.** We compared seven models and then reported the winner's confidence bands as though we had fitted only it. §7's [selection optimism](../07-validation/cross-validation.qmd) applies: the honest interval after a search is wider than the one the software prints. ::: {.callout-tip} ## Key points - **The most accurate model here was also the second most interpretable.** The GAM scored RMSE 4.08, ahead of the random forest's 4.28 and the boosted trees' 4.74, and it closed 83% of the gap between the mean-only baseline and an oracle. - The real trade-off is not accuracy against interpretability. It is **knowing the functional form against not knowing it.** The same GLM family scored 4.25 with the right form and 4.38 with linear terms. - An interpretable fit reports **effects with uncertainty**. The GAM recovered the substrate ordering, the temperature optimum to within a degree, and salinity's null effect — all things the importance measures on the previous pages got wrong or could not say. - **On depth, where the survey is confounded, the GAM produced a wide answer rather than a wrong one** — its interval covers the truth at 197 of 200 grid points and excludes zero only beyond 155 m. The forest's partial dependence, on the same data, drew a confident monotone decline with no interval at all. - Reach for a black box when the structure is not additive, when the inputs are raw, or when you do not know the form — not because you assume it will predict better. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Tune the boosted trees with `tune_grid()` over `trees`, `learn_rate` and `tree_depth`. How much of the gap to the GAM does tuning close, and how long did it take you? 2. Replace `s(longitude, latitude)` with nothing and refit the GAM. How much accuracy is in the spatial smoother alone, and what happens to the depth smooth?
